The same record's FTE and non-FTE accruals, 12,556.50 and 0.00, also add to 12,556.50 - re-performed and compared separately below, since they corroborate the figure rather than build it. explained.intro: Here is the calculation in plain language, using employee 1073 - the same record `worked_example` above is drawn from.
explained.context: The two legs are valued differently. CP (paid holiday) is a liability the business already knows in full, carried forward as last year's provision plus this year's. RTT is earned gradually over the year, so only the days not yet taken are still owed, and only a twelfth of their value is added each month - the same twelfth `methodology.notes` describes.

steps.label: RTT days earned so far
steps.detail: The yearly RTT entitlement, divided by twelve and multiplied by months worked.

steps.label: Unused RTT days
steps.detail: Days earned so far, minus days already taken, floored at zero.

steps.label: Value the unused days
steps.detail: Unused RTT days, times the employee's daily salary rate.

steps.label: A twelfth of that value
steps.detail: Only a twelfth of the RTT value is accrued this month.

steps.label: Add the paid-holiday provision
steps.detail: The CP provision, carried forward from last year plus this year.

steps.label: FTE and non-FTE employees only
steps.detail: Other staffing types fall outside this review's population.

explained.summary: In one sentence: the total accrual is one month's share of the value of unused RTT days, plus the full value of unused paid holidays, for FTE and non-FTE employees only.
caveats: The amount excludes employer social charges.
Only the RTT portion is divided by twelve; the paid-holiday amount is counted in full.
Both legs are floored at zero so a balance that has been overspent never turns an employee's accrual negative - there is no separate rule that zeroes RTT simply because none of it has been taken yet.
